fr:mainmatter.html:p: An interesting fact about Geolog as a language the reader may have noticed is that the only model of Set that one can write down in the empty context is the singleton type tuple {}.

This is remedied by inductive types. In geolog, inductive types are produced by initial models. An initial model for a theory T is a model of T that makes zero decisions: the only elements in the sets in the model are the ones forced to exist by the laws of the theory.
Recall from Sets as theories the theory PopulatedSantaList given by
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define JohnAndMary to be an initial model of PopulatedSantaList in the following way.todo (Note that here the type of JohnAndMary is inferred to be PopulatedSantaList).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def JohnAndMary := init PopulatedSantaList
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now JohnAndMary is a model of PopulatedSantaList where JohnAndMary.list.nice is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.john and JohnAndMary.list.naughty is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.mary.
The empty set is the initial model of Set.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def empty := init Set

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can use initial models in order to take the transitive closure of a graph in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
theory TransitiveExtension (@ind m : Drama) := sig transitively-jealous-of : m.person -> m.person -> Prop include : (x y : m.person) -> m.jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of x y transitive : (x y z : m.person) -> transitively-jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of y z -> transitively-jealous-of x z end
ind def TransitiveClosure (m : Drama) := init (TransitiveExtension m)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a model m of Drama, we can then access the transitive closure of m.jealous-of via TransitiveClosure m .transitively-jealous-of. The intuition here is that init (TransitiveExtension m) give us the minimal binary relation that both extends m.jealous-of and also is transitive; this is precisely the transitive closure.
We discuss why @ind m is necessary shortly.
While initial models are very powerful, they must be used carefully. First of all, not all theories have initial models.

fr:title.text: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As sets are theories, we might try to produce a point of any set via the following definition.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def something-from-nothing (A : Set) : A := init A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, this would make geolog inconsistent by allowing us to produce a point in the empty set.

Intuitively, we can not take an initial model if that would involve producing “out of nothing” elements of sets that are already defined. We can only introduce elements into sets that are in the process of being defined.
This also means that if a theory has a function whose codomain is an inductively-defined set (a set defined as part of an initial model), there is no initial model for that theory.

fr:title.text: A theory with no initial model

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A theory with no initial model

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define Or in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Or/motive (@ind p0 : Prop) (@ind p1 : Prop) := sig implicand : Prop impl0 : p0 -> implicand impl1 : p1 -> implicand end
ind def Or (p0 : Prop) (p1 : Prop) : Prop := init (Or/motive p0 p1) .implicand
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We call it Or/motive for reasons we will get into later; broadly speaking the motive is the theory one needs to provide a model of in order to use an element of Or p0 p1.
Intuitively, Or p0 p1 is the minimal proposition that is implied by both p0 and p1. Then the following has no initial model.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitively, struct { true; false; _ } and struct { false; true; _ } are both models of HardChoice, but neither one is “more minimal” than the other, and the only way to get something “more minimal” than both would be struct { false; false; _ } but this is not a model of HardChoice.
In fact, this theory would be rejected by the geolog type theory. In order to make geolog accept this theory, one must put ind in front of theory, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then this is a perfectly fine schema for a database, but we cannot take an initial model of an “inductive theory”. Sometimes we say “conjunctive theory” to refer to the normal theories, of which it is possible to take initial models.
Give more examples of initial models, explain @ind, talk about how to use element of types in initial models.
A traditional database language (or indeed general-purpose language) has many syntactic classes used for different purposes.
SQL has an exceedingly large grammar. For instance, a single SELECT statement has many possible clauses, each with their own syntax (see the postgresql manual).

Many languages have a different syntax for type parameters to a function than regular parameters. For instance, in Rust one uses Vec<i32> for applying the Vec : Type -> Type function to i32 while normal function application looks like plus(1, 2), in OCaml one uses int list while normal function application looks like plus 1 2.

Geolog differs from this, perhaps to an extreme degree, by only having essentially one syntactic class: the syntactic class of an element of a type. Even types themselves are in this syntactic class, because types are elements of type universes. What is achieved via syntactic differentiation in other languages is achieved instead by semantic restrictions in geolog.

In geolog there are set-level types, theory-level types, and top-level types. These all use the same syntax; operations which only work on set-level types will produce an error during elaboration. See Basic types for more information about this topic.

One downside of this approach is that the grammar of geolog is not a very meaningful way of getting a feel for the language; the grammar is almost trivial. What is important is understanding the semantics of geolog and the process of elaboration.

Elaboration is the process of producing syntax from notation, reporting diagnostics to the user when the user’s intent as expressed through notation is not compatible with the rules of the type theory.
Syntax is a data type in the geolog compiler, the elements of which are a compressed form for correct derivations in the geolog type theory.
The process of elaboration ensures that any syntax produced does in fact refer uniquely to some derivation.
Notation is another data type in the geolog compiler. Notation is the first “tree-shaped” data type that is produced in the compilation pipeline, and is fairly permissive in terms of what is allowed.
See fnotation for a description of the notation used in geolog.
A diagnostic is a message from the compiler to the user intended to explain a failure on the compiler’s part to fully understand the user’s intent.

Sometimes, there is a reasonable guess that the compiler can make as to how to continue, in which case the diagnostic is a “warning”—a warning that perhaps the choice the compiler is making is not what the user intended. In other cases, the compiler cannot make a reasonable guess, and the diagnostic is an “error”.

Geolog follows the philosophy of Bicameral, Not Homoiconic in using a fairly unstructured “lower house syntax” as the target of parsing (or as Krishnamurthi calls it, “reading”). We use the term “notation” as a shorthand for “lower house syntax” in order to reserve the word “syntax” for trees that compactly refer to derivations. Unlike a traditional LISP, we do not use s-expressions. Our notation is instead inspired by modern LISPs like Julia and Rhombus. We call it “f-notation” for no particular reason.
In this section, we describe f-notation.
Lexing chops up a string into tagged chunks. F-notation has the following token kinds, which we break up into categories.

A name is built up out of a sequence of name segments separated by slashes with no intervening spaces. Each name segment is comprised either of alphanumerical letters or of symbols. Hyphens may appear in symbolic name segments or alphanumerical name segments. Only the last name segment in a name may be symbolic. Examples: Monoid/is-commutative, List/::.
The slashes are eventually intended to be used for namespacing in the style of yuujinchou; this is currently not supported however.
The f-notation configuration assigns special token kinds to specific name segments.

html:tr.html:td: Alphanumerical keyword, used for reserved words that nonetheless parse normally
Symbolic identifier, used for variables, defaults to infix application
Symbolic keyword, used for reserved infix keywords that nonetheless parse normally
Used to designate a top-level declaration
Used to modify a top-level declaration

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In geolog, the special name segments and their corresponding kinds are as follows.
Names with no segment found in the above list are classified as identifiers; it is invalid to have a multi-segment name that uses a reserved name segment.
We use boldface for block tokens and decl tokens in code snippets as a very rudimentary form of syntax highlighting.
Putting . in front of a name turns it into a field, and putting ' in front of a name turns it into a tag.
Fields are intended for use in accessing a record. For instance a .b gets the b field from the record; a.b is also valid and parses the same.
Tags are intended for use in creating elements of a sum type. For instance 'just 1 could be an element of the sum type Maybe Int. Currently geolog does not have either sum types or tags, however.
F-notation has string literals with double quotes and integer literals with arabic numerals.
There is a token kind for each of (, ), [, ], {, }, ,, ;, \n, and end-of-file.
When a certain token fails to lex for whatever reason, an error token kind is inserted and lexing continues.
Whitespace is generally ignored, though newlines create \n tokens.
Line comments starting with # are considered whitespace.
From tokens, the tree structure of f-notation is fairly simple. We give the main syntactic constructs here.
Most things in f-notation are expressions, including:
The exception is declarations which may only appear in blocks; a block contains statements which are either declarations or expressions. However, a block is an expression.
Identifiers, keywords, literals, tags, and fields are all expressions.
A tuple consists of an opening bracket followed by comma-separated expressions, followed by a closing bracket. For example: [a,b,c].
Juxtaposition is two expressions next to each other, like f x. As a.b lexes as two tokens, a and .b, this is also a juxtaposition.
Infix application is two expressions with a symbolic identifier or keyword between them, like a : Int.

Juxtaposition binds tighter than infix application and left associates. Thus, f x y is (f x) y and f x + y is (f x) + y. The binding strength and associativity of infix application is determined by a custom precedence table.
The precedence table for geolog is as follows.
The only role of parentheses in f-notation is to clarify binding, so in particular parentheses are always idempotent. That is, (e) is always the same as ((e)) in every context.
A declaration consists of a declaration token followed by an expression. For example
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def x : Int := 5
fr:mainmatter.html:p: is a declaration, which could be parenthesized as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def ((x : Int) := 5)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A declaration may be modified as well by modification tokens, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: pub def x : Int := 5
fr:mainmatter.html:p: These modifiers form part of the overall declaration.
A block consists of a block token followed by either

html:ul.html:li: A newline, and then a sequence of newline-separated statements, closed by an end token.
An opening curly brace, and then a sequence of semicolon-separated statements, closed by a closing curly brace.todo

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An example of the first variant is
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: sig x : Int def x-plus-1 := x + 1 y : is-odd x-plus-1 end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: An example of the second variant is
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: sig { x : Int; def x-plus-1 := x + 1; y : is-odd x-plus-1 }
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Blocks may appear within expressions, but declarations may not; declarations may only appear within blocks.
The top level of a f-notation file is considered to be inside a block of the first variant, so it consists of a sequence of newline-separated statements.

At its core, there are only two things in the geolog language: types and elements of those types. We write a : A to express that a is an element of the type A. In this section, we describe informally the various types in geolog and how they are functionally involved in the database.

fr:title.text: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In geolog, we use the word theory to mean a type used as a database schema, and we say model to refer to an element of a theory, which you might also think of as a database instance on the schema described by that theory.

We now show how to build up progressively more complex theories via different type formers. In order to give an intuition for what each of these type formers means, we also describe how to interact with models of those theories via the TypeScript FFI (note: the TypeScript FFI is a work in progress at the moment).
Set is a theory, and models of Set are collections of things. This corresponds to a very simple kind of database by itself, but we can do many things from this foundation.
We refer to models of Set as, unsurprisingly, “sets.”
In TypeScript, models of Set store collections of Values, where Value is defined in the following way
All elements in the collection should be of the same type (e.g. all row ids, all strings, etc.) but for simplicity all sets share the same untyped API involving Values.
A TypeScript value m that refers to a model of Set satisfies the following interface
If m has read-write permissions, then it will also satisfy the interface

Intuitively, add() does not take parameters because it adds a fresh element to the set, an element not equal to any other previous element. This means that a set of integers can never be read-write because it is impossible to create a fresh integer. We will see later on that it is instead possible to store a subset of the set of all integers; this will look differently however.
For a set with read-write permission, the following code should not throw an error.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const a = m.add() assert(m.has(a))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Records types are a way of composing multiple theories into one theory. A record type has multiple fields, each of which is declared to be a model of another theory. For instance:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaList := sig naughty : Set nice : Set end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: SantaList is a very simple theory, the models of which consist of a pair of a collection of naughty things and a collection of nice things.

More precisely, if we have a model m of SantaList in TypeScript, then m.naughty and m.nice are both models of Set. If m is readonly, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadonlySet, and if m is read-write, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadWriteSet. The following TypeScript code should run without errors if m is a read-write model of SantaList.
A model A : Set may itself be used as a theory. A model of A is just an element of A (remember that a model of Set is a collection of things). For example, consider the following theory.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A model m of PopulatedSantaList consists of a model m.list of SantaList, along with specific elements m.john in m.list.nice and m.mary in m.list.naughty.
In TypeScript, an element of a set comes along with a getter, and if it is read-write, also a setter. So if m is a TypeScript variable accessing a model of PopulatedSantaList, then we should have:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: assert(m.list.nice.has(m.john.get()))
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If m is incomplete, then m.john.get() might return null. This would be the case in a freshly-created model, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = PopulatedSantaList.create()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: This can be remedied by using .set(), as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const john = m.list.nice.add() m.john.set(john)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that m.john.set(x) would throw an exception if x were not in m.list.nice.
Function types are theories, as long as the domain is a set and the codomain is a theory.
Function types can be used in many ways. Here are some examples.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory StateMachine := sig state : Set next : state -> state end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If we have m : StateMachine, then m.next is a function that sends elements of m.state to other elements of m.state. The type state -> state satisfies the criterion for being a theory because its domain is a set and its codomain is a theory (following Sets as theories). Concretely, in TypeScript, we could use this like
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = StateMachine.create() const [x,y] = [m.state.add(), m.state.add()] m.next(x).set(y) m.next(y).set(y)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that at the point where we have added x and y but not yet set the values of next for them, m is not a valid instance for StateMachine. In fact, in general it is inevitable that in the process of building a model one may pass through an invalid state. Thus, validity is only checked at certain points; we discuss validity more in a later section.todo
But that is not all functions can do. As the codomain of a function can be a theory, we could also do the following.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaLists := sig year : Set list : year -> SantaList end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, we could use a model m of SantaLists in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const y2025 = m.year.add() const bob = m.list(y2025).nice.add()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now, there are some ontological problems with this database schema. We cannot ask whether a person is nice one year and naughty the other year, because the nice and naughty sets for each year are disjoint. What we would really like is there to be one set of people, and then in different years they might be nice or naughty. This can be accomplished with relations.

There is a theory Prop which is even more boring than Set; it is the theory of a set with at most one element. One could think of it also as a truth value: inhabited means true and empty means false. From TypeScript, we have the interface

While on its own Prop is boring, we can combine it with function types to make it more interesting. For instance, we can now rewrite SantaLists so that the same person may appear on lists in different years.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory SantaListOver (person : Set) := sig naughty : person -> Prop nice : person -> Prop end
theory SantaLists := sig year : Set children : Set list : year -> SantaListOver children end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Here we have also introduced an additional feature: a theory can have parameters, which are models of other theories. In this case, SantaList now takes in a parameter person which is a model of Set. We instantiate this parameter with children in SantaLists.
In TypeScript, we could interact with a read-write model m of this new SantaLists in the following way.
We call a function whose codomain is Prop a relation. m.list(y2025).nice is a unary relation because it takes in one argument. Here is another example, this time of a binary relation.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, using a model of Drama would look like:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const [john, mary] = [m.person.add(), m.person.add()] m.jealous_of(john)(mary).makeTrue()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that because names in fnotation can contain characters like - that are not allowed in TypeScript, we have to mangle the geolog name to create the TypeScript API. As person_of is also a valid name in geolog, a theory could have both person-of and person_of fields. In this case, emitting the TypeScript FFI would emit an error. The suggested fix is to not have fields that differ only by choice of hyphen/underscore, because that is bad and confusing in any case.

Just like a set is a theory, a proposition is also a theory; a model of the proposition can be thought of as a witness that the proposition is true. We can use this to put laws in our database. For instance, we can make jealousy be transitive.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory ExtraDrama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop jealous-of/is-transitive : (a b c : person) -> jealous-of a b -> jealous-of b c -> jealous-of a c end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We saw earlier one way in which a model of a theory might be incomplete; a function might not yet be defined for given values of its inputs. Here we have a similar situation. For instance, we might have written:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const [john, mary, sue] = [m.person.add(), m.person.add(), m.person.add()] m.jealous_of(john)(mary).makeTrue() m.jealous_of(mary)(sue).makeTrue()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When checking validity of m after executing this code, geolog will report that jealous-of/is-transitive john mary sue _ _ : jealous-of mary sue is not satisfied (though, geolog does not know what names we have given to these variables in TypeScript, so it would actually print out the row identifiers instead of the names).todo Unlike with next in the section on functions, to fix this we don't need to touch jealous-of/is-transitive. Instead, we can just run m.jealous_of(john)(sue).makeTrue(), and the model will be valid again. This is because if the codomain of a function is a proposition, there is ultimately only one possible way for that function to exist, and thus the function need not be explicitly defined. We discuss how this works in a later section.todo
Another way of creating interesting propositions is with equality. Given two elements a0 and a1 of a set A, there is a proposition a0 = a1 which is true if and only if a0 is equal to a1.
We can use this to write down laws in our theories that involve equality. For instance, we can write down the theory of a two-way mapping (mathematically known as a bijection) in the following way
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory TwoWayMapping (X : Set) (Y : Set) := sig fwd : X -> Y bwd : Y -> X bwd-fwd : (x : X) -> bwd (fwd x) = x fwd-bwd : (y : Y) -> fwd (bwd x) = x end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another example of equality usage is when we assert that a relation is a partial function, by saying that if x is related to both y0 and y1 then y0 must be equal to y1.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory IsPartialFunction (X : Set) (Y : Set) (R : X -> Y -> Prop) := (x : X) -> (y0 y1 : Y) -> R x y0 -> R x y1 -> y0 = y1
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Equality is useful for constraints, but is especially useful for queries.

These six type formers (The theory of sets, Record types as theories, Sets as theories, Function types as theories, Propositions and relations and Equality types as theories) can be used to compositionally build up fairly complex combinatorial structures of sets, functions and relations. However, they are still limited when it comes to handling data, which often has, for instance, numbers and strings in it.

We could simply put in String and Int in as “base sets”. However, this would permit functions String -> String, and we cannot store a function like that in a database because the set of strings is infinite and the function must be total, so storing the value of the function at every string would take infinite storage. We could say that String was a theory and not a set, which would prevent it from being used in the domain of a function, but it is perfectly sensible to have the theory String -> Prop (which denotes a subset of the set of all strings), and making String a theory would prevent us from forming that.

The solution to this problem requires building up a little more theory, so we do not address it right now, and instead continue on to give a full account of the “purely combinatorial” fragment of geolog.

fr:title.text: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One can query a database in geolog via for-loops in TypeScript, but this is obviously not the most efficient or ergonomic way to do it. In fact, we already have the machinery to write down queries, it just requires a bit of rethinking what we have already learned. The idea is that giving a way to produce a set from a model of a theory is a query. The elements of that set are the results of the query.

Just like we have record types as the theory-level, we also have record types at the set-level. We can use this to define a set in the context of a model of a given theory; this is how to “natively query” an instance of a geolog theory.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a : m.person b : m.person c : m.person a-b : m.jealous-of a b b-c : m.jealous-of b c c-a : m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: In TypeScript, jealousy-triangle is compiled to a function that takes in a model of Drama and returns a ReadonlySet.todo The elements v of this ReadonlySet are Values with the "tuple" tag, which have fields a,b,c that are elements of m.person, such that m.jealous-of(v.value.a)(v.value.b).isTrue(), and so on. The value v will also have v.value.a_b, but it will just be null, thought of as the unique element of the singleton set.

Iterating through the elements of jealousy_triangle(m) will be faster than the naive approach of a triply-nested for-loop over m.person and then filtering out using m.jealous-of, because geolog can plan the query and take advantage of fast join algorithms on the m.jealous-of table.todo
This query can be written more compactly in the following way.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a b c : m.person m.jealous-of a b m.jealous-of b c m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can omit the field names for propositions because we never need to refer to the witnesses of the propositions, we just need the propositions to be true.
As a variation on the same theme, we could look for length-3 cycles in a state machine with
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def next-triangle (m : StateMachine) : Set := tuple a b c : m.state m.next a = b m.next b = c m.next c = a end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In the queries, we saw several usages of the pattern
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def query (m : T) : Set := ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: def is in fact a much more general construct; any theory can replace Set on the right, and we can take in multiple arguments.
In general, this allows one to create a view of a model one theory, in the form of a model of another theory.

fr:title.text: Elements of record types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of record types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If a theory is given by a record type (using sig ... end), then we can produce a model of it using struct ... end, setting all of its fields. For example, we can reward the wrong children with the following code (using SantaList from Record types as theories).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def santa-mixup (m : SantaList) : SantaList := struct naughty := m.nice nice := m.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When using struct, one must give all the fields of the original record type in the same order as they were originally defined.
With some slightly more complex code, we can produce a model of SantaList from a model of SantaLists and a choice of year.

Intuitively, this assigns naughty to the set of children naughty in that year, and similarly with nice. The tuple syntax is just as in Record types as sets, using the curly-brace inline syntax. And m.list y .naughty child is just a sequence of function applications and field projection. Walking through the types, we have m.list : m.person -> SantaListOver m.person, so m .list y : SantaListOver m.person and then m.list y .naughty : m.person -> Prop and finally m.list y .naughty child : Prop.

fr:title.text: Elements of function types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of function types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Just as we can produce elements of record types with struct ... end, we can produce elements of function types with lambda syntax x => a, just like anonymous functions in Javascript.
As an example, we can produce the graph of a function, which is a binary relation on the domain and codomain.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def graph (X : Set) (Y : Set) (f : X -> Y) : X -> Y -> Prop := x => y => f x = y
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can also now start making some non-trivial views of theories that involve function types. For instance, we could run a state-machine at double speed.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def double-time (m : StateMachine) : StateMachine := struct state := m.state next := x => m.next (m.next x) end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Basic types we learned:

html:ul.html:li: How to use theory and def. These are the only two top-level declarations in geolog, so we have now learned all of the top-level declarations.
How to use Set, Prop, sets, record types, function types and equality types to build up theories.
How to produce some models of theories from other models.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Inductive types, we will see how to produce more models of theories, which will in turn allow us to produce more theories. However, the basic structure introduced here will remain more or less the same.
An interesting fact about Geolog as a language the reader may have noticed is that the only model of Set that one can write down in the empty context is the singleton type tuple {}.

This is remedied by inductive types. In geolog, inductive types are produced by initial models. An initial model for a theory T is a model of T that makes zero decisions: the only elements in the sets in the model are the ones forced to exist by the laws of the theory.
Recall from Sets as theories the theory PopulatedSantaList given by
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define JohnAndMary to be an initial model of PopulatedSantaList in the following way.todo (Note that here the type of JohnAndMary is inferred to be PopulatedSantaList).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def JohnAndMary := init PopulatedSantaList
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now JohnAndMary is a model of PopulatedSantaList where JohnAndMary.list.nice is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.john and JohnAndMary.list.naughty is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.mary.
The empty set is the initial model of Set.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def empty := init Set

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can use initial models in order to take the transitive closure of a graph in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
theory TransitiveExtension (@ind m : Drama) := sig transitively-jealous-of : m.person -> m.person -> Prop include : (x y : m.person) -> m.jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of x y transitive : (x y z : m.person) -> transitively-jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of y z -> transitively-jealous-of x z end
ind def TransitiveClosure (m : Drama) := init (TransitiveExtension m)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a model m of Drama, we can then access the transitive closure of m.jealous-of via TransitiveClosure m .transitively-jealous-of. The intuition here is that init (TransitiveExtension m) give us the minimal binary relation that both extends m.jealous-of and also is transitive; this is precisely the transitive closure.
We discuss why @ind m is necessary shortly.
While initial models are very powerful, they must be used carefully. First of all, not all theories have initial models.

fr:title.text: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As sets are theories, we might try to produce a point of any set via the following definition.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def something-from-nothing (A : Set) : A := init A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, this would make geolog inconsistent by allowing us to produce a point in the empty set.

Intuitively, we can not take an initial model if that would involve producing “out of nothing” elements of sets that are already defined. We can only introduce elements into sets that are in the process of being defined.
This also means that if a theory has a function whose codomain is an inductively-defined set (a set defined as part of an initial model), there is no initial model for that theory.

fr:title.text: A theory with no initial model

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A theory with no initial model

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define Or in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Or/motive (@ind p0 : Prop) (@ind p1 : Prop) := sig implicand : Prop impl0 : p0 -> implicand impl1 : p1 -> implicand end
ind def Or (p0 : Prop) (p1 : Prop) : Prop := init (Or/motive p0 p1) .implicand
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We call it Or/motive for reasons we will get into later; broadly speaking the motive is the theory one needs to provide a model of in order to use an element of Or p0 p1.
Intuitively, Or p0 p1 is the minimal proposition that is implied by both p0 and p1. Then the following has no initial model.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitively, struct { true; false; _ } and struct { false; true; _ } are both models of HardChoice, but neither one is “more minimal” than the other, and the only way to get something “more minimal” than both would be struct { false; false; _ } but this is not a model of HardChoice.
In fact, this theory would be rejected by the geolog type theory. In order to make geolog accept this theory, one must put ind in front of theory, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then this is a perfectly fine schema for a database, but we cannot take an initial model of an “inductive theory”. Sometimes we say “conjunctive theory” to refer to the normal theories, of which it is possible to take initial models.
Give more examples of initial models, explain @ind, talk about how to use element of types in initial models.
In Basic types we learned:

html:ul.html:li: How to use theory and def. These are the only two top-level declarations in geolog, so we have now learned all of the top-level declarations.
How to use Set, Prop, sets, record types, function types and equality types to build up theories.
How to produce some models of theories from other models.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Inductive types, we will see how to produce more models of theories, which will in turn allow us to produce more theories. However, the basic structure introduced here will remain more or less the same.
A traditional database language (or indeed general-purpose language) has many syntactic classes used for different purposes.
SQL has an exceedingly large grammar. For instance, a single SELECT statement has many possible clauses, each with their own syntax (see the postgresql manual).

Many languages have a different syntax for type parameters to a function than regular parameters. For instance, in Rust one uses Vec<i32> for applying the Vec : Type -> Type function to i32 while normal function application looks like plus(1, 2), in OCaml one uses int list while normal function application looks like plus 1 2.

Geolog differs from this, perhaps to an extreme degree, by only having essentially one syntactic class: the syntactic class of an element of a type. Even types themselves are in this syntactic class, because types are elements of type universes. What is achieved via syntactic differentiation in other languages is achieved instead by semantic restrictions in geolog.

In geolog there are set-level types, theory-level types, and top-level types. These all use the same syntax; operations which only work on set-level types will produce an error during elaboration. See Basic types for more information about this topic.

One downside of this approach is that the grammar of geolog is not a very meaningful way of getting a feel for the language; the grammar is almost trivial. What is important is understanding the semantics of geolog and the process of elaboration.

Elaboration is the process of producing syntax from notation, reporting diagnostics to the user when the user’s intent as expressed through notation is not compatible with the rules of the type theory.
Syntax is a data type in the geolog compiler, the elements of which are a compressed form for correct derivations in the geolog type theory.
The process of elaboration ensures that any syntax produced does in fact refer uniquely to some derivation.
Notation is another data type in the geolog compiler. Notation is the first “tree-shaped” data type that is produced in the compilation pipeline, and is fairly permissive in terms of what is allowed.
See fnotation for a description of the notation used in geolog.
A diagnostic is a message from the compiler to the user intended to explain a failure on the compiler’s part to fully understand the user’s intent.

Sometimes, there is a reasonable guess that the compiler can make as to how to continue, in which case the diagnostic is a “warning”—a warning that perhaps the choice the compiler is making is not what the user intended. In other cases, the compiler cannot make a reasonable guess, and the diagnostic is an “error”.

Geolog follows the philosophy of Bicameral, Not Homoiconic in using a fairly unstructured “lower house syntax” as the target of parsing (or as Krishnamurthi calls it, “reading”). We use the term “notation” as a shorthand for “lower house syntax” in order to reserve the word “syntax” for trees that compactly refer to derivations. Unlike a traditional LISP, we do not use s-expressions. Our notation is instead inspired by modern LISPs like Julia and Rhombus. We call it “f-notation” for no particular reason.
In this section, we describe f-notation.
Lexing chops up a string into tagged chunks. F-notation has the following token kinds, which we break up into categories.

A name is built up out of a sequence of name segments separated by slashes with no intervening spaces. Each name segment is comprised either of alphanumerical letters or of symbols. Hyphens may appear in symbolic name segments or alphanumerical name segments. Only the last name segment in a name may be symbolic. Examples: Monoid/is-commutative, List/::.
The slashes are eventually intended to be used for namespacing in the style of yuujinchou; this is currently not supported however.
The f-notation configuration assigns special token kinds to specific name segments.

html:tr.html:td: Alphanumerical keyword, used for reserved words that nonetheless parse normally
Symbolic identifier, used for variables, defaults to infix application
Symbolic keyword, used for reserved infix keywords that nonetheless parse normally
Used to designate a top-level declaration
Used to modify a top-level declaration

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In geolog, the special name segments and their corresponding kinds are as follows.
Names with no segment found in the above list are classified as identifiers; it is invalid to have a multi-segment name that uses a reserved name segment.
We use boldface for block tokens and decl tokens in code snippets as a very rudimentary form of syntax highlighting.
Putting . in front of a name turns it into a field, and putting ' in front of a name turns it into a tag.
Fields are intended for use in accessing a record. For instance a .b gets the b field from the record; a.b is also valid and parses the same.
Tags are intended for use in creating elements of a sum type. For instance 'just 1 could be an element of the sum type Maybe Int. Currently geolog does not have either sum types or tags, however.
F-notation has string literals with double quotes and integer literals with arabic numerals.
There is a token kind for each of (, ), [, ], {, }, ,, ;, \n, and end-of-file.
When a certain token fails to lex for whatever reason, an error token kind is inserted and lexing continues.
Whitespace is generally ignored, though newlines create \n tokens.
Line comments starting with # are considered whitespace.
From tokens, the tree structure of f-notation is fairly simple. We give the main syntactic constructs here.
Most things in f-notation are expressions, including:
The exception is declarations which may only appear in blocks; a block contains statements which are either declarations or expressions. However, a block is an expression.
Identifiers, keywords, literals, tags, and fields are all expressions.
A tuple consists of an opening bracket followed by comma-separated expressions, followed by a closing bracket. For example: [a,b,c].
Juxtaposition is two expressions next to each other, like f x. As a.b lexes as two tokens, a and .b, this is also a juxtaposition.
Infix application is two expressions with a symbolic identifier or keyword between them, like a : Int.

Juxtaposition binds tighter than infix application and left associates. Thus, f x y is (f x) y and f x + y is (f x) + y. The binding strength and associativity of infix application is determined by a custom precedence table.
The precedence table for geolog is as follows.
The only role of parentheses in f-notation is to clarify binding, so in particular parentheses are always idempotent. That is, (e) is always the same as ((e)) in every context.
A declaration consists of a declaration token followed by an expression. For example
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def x : Int := 5
fr:mainmatter.html:p: is a declaration, which could be parenthesized as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def ((x : Int) := 5)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A declaration may be modified as well by modification tokens, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: pub def x : Int := 5
fr:mainmatter.html:p: These modifiers form part of the overall declaration.
A block consists of a block token followed by either

html:ul.html:li: A newline, and then a sequence of newline-separated statements, closed by an end token.
An opening curly brace, and then a sequence of semicolon-separated statements, closed by a closing curly brace.todo

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An example of the first variant is
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: sig x : Int def x-plus-1 := x + 1 y : is-odd x-plus-1 end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: An example of the second variant is
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: sig { x : Int; def x-plus-1 := x + 1; y : is-odd x-plus-1 }
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Blocks may appear within expressions, but declarations may not; declarations may only appear within blocks.
The top level of a f-notation file is considered to be inside a block of the first variant, so it consists of a sequence of newline-separated statements.

At its core, there are only two things in the geolog language: types and elements of those types. We write a : A to express that a is an element of the type A. In this section, we describe informally the various types in geolog and how they are functionally involved in the database.

fr:title.text: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Theories are schemas, models are instances

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In geolog, we use the word theory to mean a type used as a database schema, and we say model to refer to an element of a theory, which you might also think of as a database instance on the schema described by that theory.

We now show how to build up progressively more complex theories via different type formers. In order to give an intuition for what each of these type formers means, we also describe how to interact with models of those theories via the TypeScript FFI (note: the TypeScript FFI is a work in progress at the moment).
Set is a theory, and models of Set are collections of things. This corresponds to a very simple kind of database by itself, but we can do many things from this foundation.
We refer to models of Set as, unsurprisingly, “sets.”
In TypeScript, models of Set store collections of Values, where Value is defined in the following way
All elements in the collection should be of the same type (e.g. all row ids, all strings, etc.) but for simplicity all sets share the same untyped API involving Values.
A TypeScript value m that refers to a model of Set satisfies the following interface
If m has read-write permissions, then it will also satisfy the interface

Intuitively, add() does not take parameters because it adds a fresh element to the set, an element not equal to any other previous element. This means that a set of integers can never be read-write because it is impossible to create a fresh integer. We will see later on that it is instead possible to store a subset of the set of all integers; this will look differently however.
For a set with read-write permission, the following code should not throw an error.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const a = m.add() assert(m.has(a))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Records types are a way of composing multiple theories into one theory. A record type has multiple fields, each of which is declared to be a model of another theory. For instance:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaList := sig naughty : Set nice : Set end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: SantaList is a very simple theory, the models of which consist of a pair of a collection of naughty things and a collection of nice things.

More precisely, if we have a model m of SantaList in TypeScript, then m.naughty and m.nice are both models of Set. If m is readonly, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadonlySet, and if m is read-write, then m.naughty and m.nice will satisfy ReadWriteSet. The following TypeScript code should run without errors if m is a read-write model of SantaList.
A model A : Set may itself be used as a theory. A model of A is just an element of A (remember that a model of Set is a collection of things). For example, consider the following theory.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A model m of PopulatedSantaList consists of a model m.list of SantaList, along with specific elements m.john in m.list.nice and m.mary in m.list.naughty.
In TypeScript, an element of a set comes along with a getter, and if it is read-write, also a setter. So if m is a TypeScript variable accessing a model of PopulatedSantaList, then we should have:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: assert(m.list.nice.has(m.john.get()))
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If m is incomplete, then m.john.get() might return null. This would be the case in a freshly-created model, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = PopulatedSantaList.create()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: This can be remedied by using .set(), as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const john = m.list.nice.add() m.john.set(john)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that m.john.set(x) would throw an exception if x were not in m.list.nice.
Function types are theories, as long as the domain is a set and the codomain is a theory.
Function types can be used in many ways. Here are some examples.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory StateMachine := sig state : Set next : state -> state end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: If we have m : StateMachine, then m.next is a function that sends elements of m.state to other elements of m.state. The type state -> state satisfies the criterion for being a theory because its domain is a set and its codomain is a theory (following Sets as theories). Concretely, in TypeScript, we could use this like
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const m = StateMachine.create() const [x,y] = [m.state.add(), m.state.add()] m.next(x).set(y) m.next(y).set(y)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that at the point where we have added x and y but not yet set the values of next for them, m is not a valid instance for StateMachine. In fact, in general it is inevitable that in the process of building a model one may pass through an invalid state. Thus, validity is only checked at certain points; we discuss validity more in a later section.todo
But that is not all functions can do. As the codomain of a function can be a theory, we could also do the following.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory SantaLists := sig year : Set list : year -> SantaList end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, we could use a model m of SantaLists in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const y2025 = m.year.add() const bob = m.list(y2025).nice.add()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now, there are some ontological problems with this database schema. We cannot ask whether a person is nice one year and naughty the other year, because the nice and naughty sets for each year are disjoint. What we would really like is there to be one set of people, and then in different years they might be nice or naughty. This can be accomplished with relations.

There is a theory Prop which is even more boring than Set; it is the theory of a set with at most one element. One could think of it also as a truth value: inhabited means true and empty means false. From TypeScript, we have the interface

While on its own Prop is boring, we can combine it with function types to make it more interesting. For instance, we can now rewrite SantaLists so that the same person may appear on lists in different years.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory SantaListOver (person : Set) := sig naughty : person -> Prop nice : person -> Prop end
theory SantaLists := sig year : Set children : Set list : year -> SantaListOver children end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Here we have also introduced an additional feature: a theory can have parameters, which are models of other theories. In this case, SantaList now takes in a parameter person which is a model of Set. We instantiate this parameter with children in SantaLists.
In TypeScript, we could interact with a read-write model m of this new SantaLists in the following way.
We call a function whose codomain is Prop a relation. m.list(y2025).nice is a unary relation because it takes in one argument. Here is another example, this time of a binary relation.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: From TypeScript, using a model of Drama would look like:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const [john, mary] = [m.person.add(), m.person.add()] m.jealous_of(john)(mary).makeTrue()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that because names in fnotation can contain characters like - that are not allowed in TypeScript, we have to mangle the geolog name to create the TypeScript API. As person_of is also a valid name in geolog, a theory could have both person-of and person_of fields. In this case, emitting the TypeScript FFI would emit an error. The suggested fix is to not have fields that differ only by choice of hyphen/underscore, because that is bad and confusing in any case.

Just like a set is a theory, a proposition is also a theory; a model of the proposition can be thought of as a witness that the proposition is true. We can use this to put laws in our database. For instance, we can make jealousy be transitive.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory ExtraDrama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop jealous-of/is-transitive : (a b c : person) -> jealous-of a b -> jealous-of b c -> jealous-of a c end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We saw earlier one way in which a model of a theory might be incomplete; a function might not yet be defined for given values of its inputs. Here we have a similar situation. For instance, we might have written:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: const [john, mary, sue] = [m.person.add(), m.person.add(), m.person.add()] m.jealous_of(john)(mary).makeTrue() m.jealous_of(mary)(sue).makeTrue()
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When checking validity of m after executing this code, geolog will report that jealous-of/is-transitive john mary sue _ _ : jealous-of mary sue is not satisfied (though, geolog does not know what names we have given to these variables in TypeScript, so it would actually print out the row identifiers instead of the names).todo Unlike with next in the section on functions, to fix this we don't need to touch jealous-of/is-transitive. Instead, we can just run m.jealous_of(john)(sue).makeTrue(), and the model will be valid again. This is because if the codomain of a function is a proposition, there is ultimately only one possible way for that function to exist, and thus the function need not be explicitly defined. We discuss how this works in a later section.todo
Another way of creating interesting propositions is with equality. Given two elements a0 and a1 of a set A, there is a proposition a0 = a1 which is true if and only if a0 is equal to a1.
We can use this to write down laws in our theories that involve equality. For instance, we can write down the theory of a two-way mapping (mathematically known as a bijection) in the following way
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory TwoWayMapping (X : Set) (Y : Set) := sig fwd : X -> Y bwd : Y -> X bwd-fwd : (x : X) -> bwd (fwd x) = x fwd-bwd : (y : Y) -> fwd (bwd x) = x end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Another example of equality usage is when we assert that a relation is a partial function, by saying that if x is related to both y0 and y1 then y0 must be equal to y1.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory IsPartialFunction (X : Set) (Y : Set) (R : X -> Y -> Prop) := (x : X) -> (y0 y1 : Y) -> R x y0 -> R x y1 -> y0 = y1
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Equality is useful for constraints, but is especially useful for queries.

These six type formers (The theory of sets, Record types as theories, Sets as theories, Function types as theories, Propositions and relations and Equality types as theories) can be used to compositionally build up fairly complex combinatorial structures of sets, functions and relations. However, they are still limited when it comes to handling data, which often has, for instance, numbers and strings in it.

We could simply put in String and Int in as “base sets”. However, this would permit functions String -> String, and we cannot store a function like that in a database because the set of strings is infinite and the function must be total, so storing the value of the function at every string would take infinite storage. We could say that String was a theory and not a set, which would prevent it from being used in the domain of a function, but it is perfectly sensible to have the theory String -> Prop (which denotes a subset of the set of all strings), and making String a theory would prevent us from forming that.

The solution to this problem requires building up a little more theory, so we do not address it right now, and instead continue on to give a full account of the “purely combinatorial” fragment of geolog.

fr:title.text: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets are queries, elements are results

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One can query a database in geolog via for-loops in TypeScript, but this is obviously not the most efficient or ergonomic way to do it. In fact, we already have the machinery to write down queries, it just requires a bit of rethinking what we have already learned. The idea is that giving a way to produce a set from a model of a theory is a query. The elements of that set are the results of the query.

Just like we have record types as the theory-level, we also have record types at the set-level. We can use this to define a set in the context of a model of a given theory; this is how to “natively query” an instance of a geolog theory.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a : m.person b : m.person c : m.person a-b : m.jealous-of a b b-c : m.jealous-of b c c-a : m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: In TypeScript, jealousy-triangle is compiled to a function that takes in a model of Drama and returns a ReadonlySet.todo The elements v of this ReadonlySet are Values with the "tuple" tag, which have fields a,b,c that are elements of m.person, such that m.jealous-of(v.value.a)(v.value.b).isTrue(), and so on. The value v will also have v.value.a_b, but it will just be null, thought of as the unique element of the singleton set.

Iterating through the elements of jealousy_triangle(m) will be faster than the naive approach of a triply-nested for-loop over m.person and then filtering out using m.jealous-of, because geolog can plan the query and take advantage of fast join algorithms on the m.jealous-of table.todo
This query can be written more compactly in the following way.todo
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def jealousy-triangle (m : Drama) : Set := tuple a b c : m.person m.jealous-of a b m.jealous-of b c m.jealous-of c a end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can omit the field names for propositions because we never need to refer to the witnesses of the propositions, we just need the propositions to be true.
As a variation on the same theme, we could look for length-3 cycles in a state machine with
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def next-triangle (m : StateMachine) : Set := tuple a b c : m.state m.next a = b m.next b = c m.next c = a end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In the queries, we saw several usages of the pattern
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def query (m : T) : Set := ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: def is in fact a much more general construct; any theory can replace Set on the right, and we can take in multiple arguments.
In general, this allows one to create a view of a model one theory, in the form of a model of another theory.

fr:title.text: Elements of record types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of record types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If a theory is given by a record type (using sig ... end), then we can produce a model of it using struct ... end, setting all of its fields. For example, we can reward the wrong children with the following code (using SantaList from Record types as theories).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def santa-mixup (m : SantaList) : SantaList := struct naughty := m.nice nice := m.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: When using struct, one must give all the fields of the original record type in the same order as they were originally defined.
With some slightly more complex code, we can produce a model of SantaList from a model of SantaLists and a choice of year.

Intuitively, this assigns naughty to the set of children naughty in that year, and similarly with nice. The tuple syntax is just as in Record types as sets, using the curly-brace inline syntax. And m.list y .naughty child is just a sequence of function applications and field projection. Walking through the types, we have m.list : m.person -> SantaListOver m.person, so m .list y : SantaListOver m.person and then m.list y .naughty : m.person -> Prop and finally m.list y .naughty child : Prop.

fr:title.text: Elements of function types as views

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Elements of function types as views

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Just as we can produce elements of record types with struct ... end, we can produce elements of function types with lambda syntax x => a, just like anonymous functions in Javascript.
As an example, we can produce the graph of a function, which is a binary relation on the domain and codomain.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def graph (X : Set) (Y : Set) (f : X -> Y) : X -> Y -> Prop := x => y => f x = y
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can also now start making some non-trivial views of theories that involve function types. For instance, we could run a state-machine at double speed.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: def double-time (m : StateMachine) : StateMachine := struct state := m.state next := x => m.next (m.next x) end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Basic types we learned:

html:ul.html:li: How to use theory and def. These are the only two top-level declarations in geolog, so we have now learned all of the top-level declarations.
How to use Set, Prop, sets, record types, function types and equality types to build up theories.
How to produce some models of theories from other models.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Inductive types, we will see how to produce more models of theories, which will in turn allow us to produce more theories. However, the basic structure introduced here will remain more or less the same.
An interesting fact about Geolog as a language the reader may have noticed is that the only model of Set that one can write down in the empty context is the singleton type tuple {}.

This is remedied by inductive types. In geolog, inductive types are produced by initial models. An initial model for a theory T is a model of T that makes zero decisions: the only elements in the sets in the model are the ones forced to exist by the laws of the theory.
Recall from Sets as theories the theory PopulatedSantaList given by
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory PopulatedSantaList := sig list : SantaList john : list.nice mary : list.naughty end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define JohnAndMary to be an initial model of PopulatedSantaList in the following way.todo (Note that here the type of JohnAndMary is inferred to be PopulatedSantaList).
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def JohnAndMary := init PopulatedSantaList
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now JohnAndMary is a model of PopulatedSantaList where JohnAndMary.list.nice is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.john and JohnAndMary.list.naughty is a set that only contains JohnAndMary.mary.
The empty set is the initial model of Set.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def empty := init Set

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can use initial models in order to take the transitive closure of a graph in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Drama := sig person : Set jealous-of : person -> person -> Prop end
theory TransitiveExtension (@ind m : Drama) := sig transitively-jealous-of : m.person -> m.person -> Prop include : (x y : m.person) -> m.jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of x y transitive : (x y z : m.person) -> transitively-jealous-of x y -> transitively-jealous-of y z -> transitively-jealous-of x z end
ind def TransitiveClosure (m : Drama) := init (TransitiveExtension m)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a model m of Drama, we can then access the transitive closure of m.jealous-of via TransitiveClosure m .transitively-jealous-of. The intuition here is that init (TransitiveExtension m) give us the minimal binary relation that both extends m.jealous-of and also is transitive; this is precisely the transitive closure.
We discuss why @ind m is necessary shortly.
While initial models are very powerful, they must be used carefully. First of all, not all theories have initial models.

fr:title.text: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The theory of a point does not have an initial model.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: As sets are theories, we might try to produce a point of any set via the following definition.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind def something-from-nothing (A : Set) : A := init A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: However, this would make geolog inconsistent by allowing us to produce a point in the empty set.

Intuitively, we can not take an initial model if that would involve producing “out of nothing” elements of sets that are already defined. We can only introduce elements into sets that are in the process of being defined.
This also means that if a theory has a function whose codomain is an inductively-defined set (a set defined as part of an initial model), there is no initial model for that theory.

fr:title.text: A theory with no initial model

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A theory with no initial model

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can define Or in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory Or/motive (@ind p0 : Prop) (@ind p1 : Prop) := sig implicand : Prop impl0 : p0 -> implicand impl1 : p1 -> implicand end
ind def Or (p0 : Prop) (p1 : Prop) : Prop := init (Or/motive p0 p1) .implicand
fr:mainmatter.html:p: We call it Or/motive for reasons we will get into later; broadly speaking the motive is the theory one needs to provide a model of in order to use an element of Or p0 p1.
Intuitively, Or p0 p1 is the minimal proposition that is implied by both p0 and p1. Then the following has no initial model.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitively, struct { true; false; _ } and struct { false; true; _ } are both models of HardChoice, but neither one is “more minimal” than the other, and the only way to get something “more minimal” than both would be struct { false; false; _ } but this is not a model of HardChoice.
In fact, this theory would be rejected by the geolog type theory. In order to make geolog accept this theory, one must put ind in front of theory, as in
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: ind theory HardChoice := sig likes-bananas : Prop likes-apples : Prop at-least-one : Or likes-bananas likes-apples end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then this is a perfectly fine schema for a database, but we cannot take an initial model of an “inductive theory”. Sometimes we say “conjunctive theory” to refer to the normal theories, of which it is possible to take initial models.
Give more examples of initial models, explain @ind, talk about how to use element of types in initial models.
